props.title: L'Enfance Nue
props.initialSlug: Abandoned boy's raw journey through foster homes

sections.content: Maurice Pialat's devastating debut L'Enfance Nue (1968) revolutionized the portrayal of troubled youth in cinema through its unflinching realism and documentary-like approach. Unlike the romanticized orphan tales that came before, like Oliver! (1968) or Great Expectations (1946), Pialat strips away sentimentality to show foster child François's raw emotional state and destructive behaviors. The film's influence echoes through later works like The 400 Blows (1959) and Kes (1969), establishing a new framework for depicting childhood trauma on screen.

sections.content: Pialat's revolutionary use of non-professional actors, particularly Michel Terrazon as François, created a documentary-like authenticity that influenced generations of filmmakers. This approach can be traced through works like Rosetta (1999) by the Dardenne brothers and Fish Tank (2009) by Andrea Arnold, where untrained young performers bring raw authenticity to stories of youth in crisis. The film's influence on French cinema's portrayal of childhood continues through works like Ponette (1996) and Small Change (1976).

The film's unflinching look at institutional care and foster systems broke new ground in social realist cinema. This legacy carries through to contemporary works like Short Term 12 (2013) and System Crasher (2019), which similarly examine the complex relationships between troubled children and their caregivers. Pialat's resistance to easy solutions or moral judgments set a template for honest examination of social issues. SUBHEAD: Impact on Social Realist Cinema

sections.content: L'Enfance Nue's influence extends beyond its immediate subject matter into broader social realist filmmaking. Its technique of mixing professional and non-professional actors, use of real locations, and attention to working-class life influenced filmmakers like Ken Loach, whose Ladybird Ladybird (1994) and I, Daniel Blake (2016) carry similar documentary-like authenticity. The film's impact on depicting institutional systems continues through works like Capernaum (2018) and Les Misérables (2019).
